title: The Word's Manifestation Expands Worship to All Nations
english: So the arrangement of these songs followed the same order. After the prayer for Israel came thanksgiving, and hymns were proclaimed beforehand, and acts of worship toward God. For by his mercy and truth, because of the glory of the word of God above every name of his—that is, what has now been accomplished—God is glorified in the name of the Word as he was never glorified before. Before the manifestation of the Word, the worship of God occupied only a portion of the earth. He was hymned as maker of all things, and he was proclaimed as the God of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, but all of this had its knowledge and honor only as far as the Hebrew nation. But when his living oracle appeared, coming forth from God and revealed to the world through a body, then every nation and the whole inhabited world runs together to the worship of God, serves the name of the Word, and glorifies God in the presence of the Word. Now worship has increased among the nations according to mercy, and it is preserved for Israel according to the truth of the promises.

Psalm 137 (138):3. He shows the great favor and the swift obedience, and the supply of power given to souls in the name of Christ. For Christ says, "If you ask anything in my name, I will do it" (John 14:13). And the apostle says that the supply of the Spirit comes to those who believe.

Psalm 137 (138):5. Let the providence of God be hymned, because God is great and his greatness is revealed through providence. Just as through the seraphim the glory of God in his present providence and economy was hymned when they cried out, saying, "Holy, holy, holy, Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory" (Isaiah 6:3).

Psalm 137 (138):6. Because, he says, the human creation enjoys the gift of God, and the lesser and formerly more dishonored part of it—the nations—is not now overlooked either. For to God all things are lowly, even the highest, so that these too are known by him from afar, because they cannot draw near to the unapproachable height of God. Since all things are small before God, it is no wonder if he extends his benefits even to the smallest—that is, to those who had no hope and were without God in the world, whom the apostle calls "those who are not."

Psalm 137 (138):7–8a. He brings in the second part, the portion of Israel, which has been caught up in afflictions but will be restored to salvation. Through this your enemies are struck by God, and they themselves will obtain salvation from God. "The Lord will repay on my behalf." For he will repay on behalf of the wronged nation, so as to rescue them from the hands of those who oppress them.
Psalm 137 (138):8c. Even if, he says, we do not produce fruits worthy of your love, yet because we are your works, we ask not to be overlooked.

Psalm 138 (139):5. Here he appears to place soul and body together as one, arranging both under a single formation, because he says that God has knowledge of the soul's properties from its formation. Just as another has said, "He who formed the spirit of man within him" (Zechariah 12:1). For the work is not divided. Even if the making of the soul is more beautiful than that of the body, it is not as if made by hands according to the shaping of matter, but inspired according to its subsistence from divine power.

orientation: Apollinaris is explaining how the sequence of the psalms mirrors the spread of God's worship from Israel alone to all nations through the incarnate Word.

title: The whole person, known and formed by God
english: At any rate, he brings both together into one, just as they also share a single name, the combined thing being called sometimes soul and sometimes flesh. So too when the apostle calls the man the image of God because of the inbreathing that came to him from God and did not come upon the woman, he clearly includes the body together with the soul, insofar as the male is distinguished from the female.

Psalm 138 (139):9–10. This is just what appeared in the case of Jonah, when he fled to the sea and found God's power at work both in the movement of the waters, stirring up waves, and in the nature of the creatures: the sea-monster received him and did not crush him, and he was kept safe inside the sea-monster and suffered no corruption.

Psalm 138 (139):15–16. You know my very subsistence, he says, and the composition of my bones is your work. In the hidden place of my mother's womb, as if within the earth, you knew me as one intricately wrought even before I was formed. And I am written by you as in a book, and every human being who is fashioned is measured by a fixed time and a set number of days. This is indeed the wonder of the order and precise symmetry: that the production of life is brought to completion with not a single day lacking.

Psalm 138 (139):17–18. I did not think, he says, that the righteous were few, even though at any given time only a small number are found. Rather, I looked to the whole multitude that has existed from eternity, and I saw that they are many and greater in number, whom the resurrection will display all together—and especially now, when they have increased into a multitude at the coming of Christ, according to the words, "The whole earth is filled with the knowledge of the Lord," and "I will give thanks to you in the great church; in a heavy people I will praise you."

Psalm 138 (139):23–24. Since righteous men are precious in your sight and are laid up for eternal glory, while the wicked are destined for destruction, I beseech you that I may be cleansed from all wickedness by the cleansing that comes from you, who are able to purify us even when we fall into evil through ignorance. I pray that you cleanse me, he says, from every evil that leads to destruction and lead me through good deeds, for which eternal life will be given.

Psalm 139:9 (140:8). What is said is worthy of God: that lawlessness be given no proud thought and no exaltation against righteousness, and that their bitter and destructive purpose not come to fulfillment nor be permitted to prevail over those against whom they hold their bitterness. For when injustice succeeds, it becomes far more grievous and grows into blasphemy against the God of righteousness.

Psalm 139:11 (140:10). And they will fall a fall—not the kind the righteous fall when they fall and rise again, but the incurable kind that no longer comes to resurrection. They will depart into obscurity, unable to become established on the earth, but driven out from it into destructive punishments.

Psalm 140 (141):2. If by morning we understand the life that is coming, the life of rest and glory for the righteous, then let us understand the present life as night and evening—evening because it retains something of light through the remaining knowledge of the good and because of the gifts from God, and night because of the darkness of wickedness and the domination of the world-rulers of darkness.

title: Prayer, separation from the wicked, and the unity of God and Lord
english: So now a person needs intense crying out, because he has been pressed in by darkness and weighed down by the evils that surround him. He cries to the only one who can give light, who can show dawn out of evening and day out of night, and who can bring about a change from these evils.
He speaks, then, against wickedness, wanting to be pure from it and a stranger to those who live in it. For the wounds of friends are more trustworthy than willing kisses of enemies.

They mock what is good, he says, and disparage what is by common agreement the most beautiful thing of all—prayer—twisting it to suit their own will. And this, he says, will destroy them, uprooted from the earth, as if dug out, with a rock pushing through and dislodging their rooting. They made my words a laughingstock and a pleasure, mocking what is holy because they delight in what is unholy, and because their long habit in these things has cut off their asking for what is good and truly lovely and delightful. Second, he speaks of the sorrow of death, describing the dissolution of a human being: like a clod of earth breaking apart, he is scattered.

Symmachus says: 'Let the lawless fall into their own nets.' Let their schemes, he says, turn against them and not against us who are innocent. But I, he says, will turn aside from mixing with the wicked, until I am able to escape them altogether. For this is the safeguard against being harmed by them at all: not to come near them or be entangled with them. Jeremiah also says this: 'It is good for a man when he bears the yoke in his youth; he will sit alone and be silent' (Lamentations 3:27-28). But for us now the separation from the wicked is spiritual, because a bodily separation is impossible, since we would have to go out of the world, as Paul says.

The unity of the dyad is beautiful when it places the Lord and God in such a relation, but for those who have learned the perfect things, the comprehension of the dyad in the unity is more revealing. Paul presents this when he expounds one God and one Lord, and unites the two, who are two, so that God is understood in the Lord and the Lord in God. In this way the properties of the divine and lordly essence are seen in identity, proceeding from the Father to the Son according to what is divine, and led back from the Son to God according to what is lordly.
He does not set as the goal the escape from the siege of enemies, but something still more beautiful: to offer thanks to God. For this is indeed the highest goal.

Others say the psalm is not without a title, but is inscribed: 'A Psalm of David, when his son pursued him.' This is not found, however, in all the versions. But what is said is not foreign to it; and nothing prevents these words from having been spoken about the persecution by Saul.

Or, according to the whole theme of the life of the righteous, he does not yet receive the perfect mercy now, but awaits the future appearing from heaven that announces the morning, when the Master will shine upon the righteous, appearing from heaven.
He asks that the name of goodness become for him the occasion of God's salvation, according to the apostle who says: 'To the praise of the glory of his grace' (Ephesians 1:6).
